lesson.title: dx vs. dy: Choosing the Variable You Integrate Against
lesson.summary: The dx (or dy, or dt) at the end of an integral names the variable of integration, telling you which letter is changing while every other letter is treated as a constant.
lesson.body:
In integral notation, the piece at the very end, most often written dx, is called the variable of integration. It specifies exactly which variable in the integrand is being treated as the changing quantity, the same role that x plays when you write dy/dx for an ordinary derivative.

When an integrand only involves one letter, this choice feels automatic: of course you integrate 3x^2 with respect to x, since x is the only variable present. The variable of integration becomes essential, though, once an integrand contains more than one letter. In that situation, dx tells you to treat x as the variable and every other letter as if it were a fixed constant, while dy would tell you to do the opposite.

Consider the integrand 6xy^2, which contains both x and y. If we integrate with respect to x, we write ∫6xy^2 dx, and y^2 is held constant throughout: pull it out front as 6y^2 · ∫x dx = 6y^2 · (x^2/2) = 3x^2y^2 + C. Check this by differentiating with respect to x while treating y as constant: d/dx[3x^2y^2] = 6xy^2, which matches the integrand.

Now integrate the very same integrand with respect to y instead: ∫6xy^2 dy. This time x is held constant, so pull it out front as 6x · ∫y^2 dy = 6x · (y^3/3) = 2xy^3 + C. Checking by differentiating with respect to y while treating x as constant: d/dy[2xy^3] = 2x · 3y^2 = 6xy^2, again matching the integrand. Notice that the same integrand produced two genuinely different answers, 3x^2y^2 + C versus 2xy^3 + C, purely because the variable of integration changed. This is exactly why the dx or dy at the end of an integral is never decorative: it is an instruction that changes the outcome, so it must always be read as part of the notation, never skipped.
